column2:
yīnyùnxué
The study of the sound systems of Chinese in each period and how they changed; a branch of traditional philology.

shànggǔyīn
Pre-Qin and Han Chinese pronunciation, reconstructed mainly from Shijing rhymes and phonetic series.

zhōnggǔyīn
Sui–Tang Chinese as recorded in the Qieyun family of rhyme dictionaries and the early rhyme tables.

jìndàiyīn
Yuan–Qing Chinese, represented by works such as the Zhongyuan yinyun.

gǔyīnxué
The study of Old Chinese phonology.

jīnyīnxué
The study of the Qieyun sound system.

děngyùnxué
The study of rhyme tables and of syllable structure.

nǐyīn
A reconstructed pronunciation, usually marked with an asterisk *.

gòunǐ
Inferring earlier sound forms by the comparative method, internal reconstruction and similar methods.

Qièyùn
Rhyme dictionary compiled by Lu Fayan and others in 601; the foundation of Middle Chinese studies.

Guǎngyùn
The Da Song chongxiu Guangyun, revised by Chen Pengnian and others in 1008; it has 206 rhymes.

Jíyùn
Rhyme dictionary compiled by Ding Du and others in 1039, with more characters than the Guangyun.

Yùnjìng
One of the oldest surviving rhyme tables, in 43 charts.

Qīyīnlüè
The rhyme tables in Zheng Qiao's Tongzhi, in 43 charts.

Qièyùn Zhǐzhǎngtú
A Song-dynasty set of rhyme tables in 20 charts.

Jīngdiǎn Shìwén
Lu Deming's glosses on the classics; its many fanqie spellings make it a key Middle Chinese source.

Shuōwén Jiězì
Xu Shen's dictionary; its analysis of phono-semantic characters underlies the study of phonetic series.

Shījīng
The pre-Qin anthology of poems; its rhymes are the main evidence for Old Chinese rhyme groups.

shēngmǔ
The consonant at the start of a syllable.

yùnmǔ
The part of a syllable after the initial: medial, main vowel and coda.

shēngdiào
Pitch distinctions that keep words apart.

shēngniǔ
Traditional name for the initial, also called niǔ.

zìmǔ
Representative characters used to name initials, as in the 36 initials.

sānshíliù zìmǔ
The Tang–Song system naming the initials with 36 representative characters.

Shǒuwēn zìmǔ
The 30 initials traditionally attributed to the late-Tang monk Shouwen.

wǔyīn
The division of initials by place of articulation into labial, lingual, dental, velar and laryngeal.

qīyīn
The five classes plus the semi-lingual and semi-dental.

chúnyīn
Labials: the bilabials 幫滂並明 and the labiodentals 非敷奉微.

zhòngchúnyīn
The bilabials 幫滂並明.

qīngchúnyīn
The labiodentals 非敷奉微, which split off from the bilabials before Division-III rounded finals.

shéyīn
Tongue initials: the shetou and sheshang series.

shétóuyīn
The dental stops and nasal 端透定泥.

shéshàngyīn
The retroflex stops and nasal 知徹澄孃.

chǐyīn
Sibilant initials: the chitou and zhengchi series.

chǐtóuyīn
The dental affricates and fricatives 精清從心邪.

zhèngchǐyīn
照穿牀審禪, further divided into the Zhuang group (照二) and the Zhang group (照三).

yáyīn
The velars 見溪羣疑.

hóuyīn
The laryngeals 影曉匣喻.

bànshéyīn
The initial 來 (l-).

bànchǐyīn
The initial 日.

qīngzhuó
The fourfold classification of initials by voicing and aspiration.

quánqīng
Unaspirated voiceless stops and affricates, and voiceless fricatives: 幫端見精心 and others.

cìqīng
Aspirated voiceless stops and affricates: 滂透溪清 and others.

quánzhuó
Voiced stops, affricates and fricatives: 並定羣從邪匣 and others.

cìzhuó
Sonorants such as nasals, laterals and glides: 明泥疑來日以云 and others.

jièyīn
The glide between initial and main vowel, such as -i- or -u-.

zhǔyuányīn
The nucleus vowel of the final, also called yùnfù.

yùnfù
Another name for the main vowel.

yùnwěi
The consonant or vowel that ends the final.

yùntóu
Another name for the medial.

yīnshēngyùn
Finals that are open or end in a vowel.

yángshēngyùn
Finals ending in a nasal: -m, -n or -ŋ.

rùshēngyùn
Finals ending in a stop: -p, -t or -k.

yīnyáng duìzhuǎn
Alternation or loan use between open, nasal and stop finals that share a main vowel.

duìzhuǎn
Alternation between rhyme groups with the same vowel but a different type of coda.

pángzhuǎn
Alternation between rhyme groups with the same type of coda and similar vowels.

tōngzhuǎn
A general term for looser rhyming or alternation between rhyme groups.

yùn
The rhyming unit of a rhyme dictionary; the Guangyun has 206.

yùnmù
The heading character of each rhyme, such as 東, 董, 送, 屋.

yùnbù
A class induced from Old Chinese rhyming, such as 之部 or 魚部.

yùnxì
A set of rhymes matched across the four tones, such as 東董送屋.

yùnlèi
Classes of finals found by linking the lower fanqie characters.

shè
In the rhyme tables, a large class of rhymes with the same coda and similar vowels; there are 16.

shíliù shè
The sixteen shè: 通江止遇蟹臻山效果假宕梗曾流深咸.

děng
The four divisions, I to IV, into which the rhyme tables sort finals.

děnghū
Division and openness taken together.

kāikǒu
Finals without -u- or lip rounding.

hékǒu
Finals with -u- or lip rounding.

kāihé
Open (kāikǒu) versus rounded (hékǒu) finals.

zhuǎn
The unit of the Yunjing and Qiyinlüe tables; one zhuǎn is one chart.

nèizhuǎn
A chart with no independent Division-II rhyme.

wàizhuǎn
A chart with an independent Division-II rhyme.

chóngniǔ
In rhymes such as 支脂祭真仙宵侵鹽, labial, velar and laryngeal syllables fall into two classes placed in Divisions III and IV.

column1:
重紐三等
Rhyme tables
column2:
chóngniǔ sānděng
Type B, placed in Division III of the tables.

column1:
重紐四等
Rhyme tables
column2:
chóngniǔ sìděng
Type A, placed in Division IV of the tables.

jiǎ sìděng
Division-III syllables placed in the Division-IV row, such as those with Jing-group or 以 initials.

jiǎ èrděng
Division-III Zhuang-group syllables placed in the Division-II row.

píngshēng
One of the four Middle Chinese tones: level.

shǎngshēng
One of the four tones: rising. Here 上 is read shǎng.

qùshēng
One of the four tones: departing.

rùshēng
One of the four tones: entering, ending in -p, -t or -k.

sìshēng
Level, rising, departing and entering.

sìshēng xiāngchéng
The matching of the level, rising, departing and entering rhymes of one set.

píngzè
The contrast between level and oblique (rising, departing, entering) tones.

fǎnqiè
Spelling a syllable with two characters: the first gives the initial, the second the final and tone.

fǎnqiè shàngzì
The first fanqie character, which gives the initial.

fǎnqiè xiàzì
The second fanqie character, which gives the final and tone.

xiǎoyùn
A group of homophones in a rhyme dictionary, headed by one character with a fanqie.

zhíyīn
Indicating a reading by citing a homophone.

dúruò
A Han-period gloss, "read like", citing a similar-sounding character.

xìliánfǎ
Chen Li's method of linking fanqie characters into classes.

xiéshēng
The sound relation between a phono-semantic character and its phonetic.

shēngfú
The component of a character that indicates its sound.

xiéshēng xìliè
The set of characters sharing one phonetic component.

tóngyuáncí
Words related in sound and meaning that come from one root.

tōngjiǎ
Writing a word with a homophonous or near-homophonous character instead of its proper one.

yāyùn
Placing characters of the same rhyme at the ends of lines.

héyùn
Occasional rhyming between different rhyme groups.

gǔ wú qīngchúnyīn
Qian Daxin's thesis: Old Chinese had no labiodentals, and 非敷奉微 were read like 幫滂並明.

gǔ wú shéshàngyīn
Qian Daxin's thesis: Old Chinese had no retroflex stops, and 知徹澄 were read like 端透定.

niáng rì guī ní
Zhang Binglin's thesis: 娘 and 日 go back to 泥 in Old Chinese.

yù sān guī xiá
Zeng Yunqian's thesis: 喻 of Division III, that is 云, goes back to 匣.

yù sì guī dìng
Zeng Yunqian's thesis: 喻 of Division IV, that is 以, was close to 定 in Old Chinese.

zhào èr guī jīng
Huang Kan's thesis: the Zhuang group goes back to the Jing group.

zhào sān guī duān
A thesis based on the frequent phonetic links between the Zhang and Duan groups; formulations differ.

gǔ wú qùshēng
Duan Yucai's thesis: Old Chinese had no departing tone.

gǔ wú shǎng qù
Huang Kan's thesis: Old Chinese had only the level and entering tones. Disputed.

tóng shēng bì tóng bù
Duan Yucai's principle: characters with the same phonetic belong to the same rhyme group.

chángrù
Wang Li's thesis: Old Chinese entering-tone syllables were long or short, and the long ones became departing tone.

liù yuányīn xìtǒng
The hypothesis of six Old Chinese vowels *i, *e, *a, *o, *u, *ə; some write *ɯ for *ə.

yānhuà
Baxter and Sagart account for non-Division-III Middle Chinese syllables with pharyngealized initials *Cˤ.

A xíng yīnjié
In Baxter–Sagart, a pharyngealized syllable; it mostly becomes Division I, II or IV.

B xíng yīnjié
In Baxter–Sagart, a non-pharyngealized syllable; it becomes Division III.

chángduǎn yuányīn
Zhengzhang and Pan derive Divisions I, II and IV from long vowels and Division III from short ones.

diànjièyīn
Medials such as -r-, -l- and -j- in Zhengzhang's system.

qiánzhuì
Old Chinese prefixes such as *s-, *m-, *N-, *k-, *t-.

hòuzhuì
Old Chinese suffixes such as *-s and *-ʔ.

cìyào yīnjié
In Baxter–Sagart, a weak syllable before the main syllable, such as *Cə.

qīngbíyīn
Old Chinese voiceless sonorants such as *m̥, *n̥, *ŋ̊; they become voiceless initials such as 曉 and 透.

fùfǔyīn
Consonant clusters in Old Chinese initials, such as *kr- and *pl-.

shēngdiào qǐyuán
Haudricourt's thesis: the rising tone arose from *-ʔ and the departing tone from *-s.

Bái Yīpíng
William H. Baxter.

Shā Jiā'ěr
Laurent Sagart.

Zhèngzhāng Shàngfāng
Author of Shanggu yinxi.

Pān Wùyún
A researcher of Old Chinese phonology.

Wáng Lì
Author of Hanyu shigao and Shijing yundu; he set up the 30 Old Chinese rhyme groups.

Gāo Běnhàn
Bernhard Karlgren.

Lǐ Fāngguì
Author of Shanggu yin yanjiu.

Dǒng Tónghé
Author of Shanggu yinyun biaogao.

Lù Fǎyán
Compiler of the Qieyun.

Chén Lǐ
Author of Qieyun kao, who devised the linking method.

Qián Dàxīn
Qing scholar who argued that antiquity had no labiodentals and no retroflex stops.

Duàn Yùcái
Author of Shuowen jiezi zhu and Liushu yinjun biao.
